title: 22. Interview: REST API
summary: Interview Q&A for REST API — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 REST API interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What are the six constraints of REST, and why does each one matter?
**Answer:** (1) **Client-server** — separation of UI concerns from data storage lets them evolve and scale independently; the client can be rewritten without touching the server. (2) **Stateless** — every request contains all context the server needs; the server holds no session state between requests, so any backend instance can serve any request, enabling horizontal scaling without session affinity. (3) **Cacheable** — responses explicitly declare cacheability (`Cache-Control`, `ETag`), letting CDNs and reverse proxies serve subsequent requests without touching the origin, dramatically reducing origin load. (4) **Uniform interface** — HTTP methods have fixed semantics (GET is safe, PUT/DELETE are idempotent) and status codes have fixed meaning (200/201/204/400/404/422/500), so any client can interact with any REST API without learning a new contract. (5) **Layered** — a client cannot tell whether it is talking to the origin or to a proxy/CDN/gateway in front of it, letting you insert load balancers, caches, and security layers without changing the client. (6) **Code-on-demand** (optional) — the server can ship executable code (JavaScript) to the client; browsers use this, but API clients rarely do. Stripe and GitHub's APIs honor all six except code-on-demand.
**Visual:**
```
Client-Server:    client <--HTTP--> server (separated concerns)
Stateless:        req1 = {auth, params}   (no server-side session)
Cacheable:        GET /v1/users -> Cache-Control: max-age=60
Uniform iface:    GET safe; PUT/DELETE idempotent; POST neither
Layered:          client -> CDN -> ALB -> service (transparent to client)
Code-on-demand:   server can send <script> to browser (optional)
```

### Q2. What is idempotency in REST, and how do you make POST safe to retry?
**Answer:** An operation is **idempotent** if calling it once has the same effect as calling it N times. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP spec — GETting the same resource twice returns the same response without side effects; PUTting the same state twice leaves the resource in the same final state; DELETEing the same resource twice either succeeds or returns 404, with no further mutation. POST is **not** idempotent — POSTing the same payload twice creates two resources. This is a problem for payment creation, order submission, and any other write that must survive network retries. The Stripe pattern: the client sends an `Idempotency-Key` header (a UUID generated client-side) with each POST; the server stores the key in Redis with a 24-hour TTL and the response body; if a retry arrives with the same key, the server returns the original response without re-executing the operation. This makes POST safe to retry even on unreliable networks. The trade-off: the server must store the response for the TTL window (memory cost), and the client must generate unique keys per logical operation (a stale key on retries is correct; reusing a key for a new operation is a bug).
**Visual:**
```
Client retries POST /v1/charges (network timeout after first attempt):

  POST /v1/charges                  POST /v1/charges
  Idempotency-Key: abc-123          Idempotency-Key: abc-123
  body: {amount: 1000}              body: {amount: 1000}
        |                                 |
        v                                 v
  server: store key=abc-123 -> charge_xxx, 201
  server: detect key=abc-123 already used -> return same 201 + charge_xxx
  (no double-charge, client gets the original response)
```

### Q3. How do you version a REST API, and what are the trade-offs of each approach?
**Answer:** Three common strategies. (1) **URL versioning** (`/v1/users`, `/v2/users`) — simplest, explicit in every request, easy to route at the proxy layer, and cacheable by URL. Downside: changing the version creates a new URL namespace, breaking existing client bookmarks and external integrations. Used by Stripe (`/v1/`), GitHub (`/v3/`), and most public APIs. (2) **Header versioning** (`Accept: application/vnd.example.v2+json`) — keeps URLs clean, lets the same resource have multiple representations, and is more REST-purist. Downside: hard to test in a browser address bar, harder to cache (CDNs key on URL, not headers), and tooling support is weaker. Used by GitHub's media-type versioning for some endpoints. (3) **Query-param versioning** (`?version=2`) — avoid. It pollutes the URL, breaks caching (the same URL with different query strings is a different cache key for some intermediaries), and is easy for clients to forget. Most production teams settle on URL versioning for clarity and tooling support, even though purists prefer header versioning. Deprecation policy matters: maintain old versions for at least 12–18 months, emit `Deprecation` and `Sunset` HTTP headers, and log usage by version to know when you can finally turn v1 off.
**Visual:**
```
URL versioning:    GET /v1/users    GET /v2/users   (different paths)
Header versioning: GET /users  +  Accept: application/vnd.x.v2+json
Query versioning:  GET /users?version=2   (avoid - breaks caching)

Recommended: URL versioning (explicit, cacheable, tooling-friendly)
```

### Q4. What is HATEOAS, and why is it rarely used in practice?
**Answer:** HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is the strictest REST constraint: the server returns hypermedia links in every response, and the client drives state transitions by following those links, never hardcoding URLs. A HATEOAS response looks like `{"id": 42, "name": "Ada", "_links": {"self": "/users/42", "orders": "/users/42/orders", "delete": {"href": "/users/42", "method": "DELETE"}}}`. The client reads `_links` to discover what actions are possible, then follows the link — the same way a browser navigates the web by clicking links, never typing URLs. The appeal: clients and servers are fully decoupled; the server can restructure its URL space without breaking clients, because clients follow links rather than hardcoded paths. In practice, HATEOAS is rarely implemented because (1) it doubles response payload size with link metadata, (2) most API clients are tightly coupled to a single server anyway, so the decoupling benefit is theoretical, (3) tooling and SDK generators rarely handle hypermedia well, (4) testing requires actually walking the link graph rather than just hitting a known URL. Spring Data REST auto-generates HATEOAS, and some payment APIs (PayPal's older API) used it. Most production APIs sit at Richardson Maturity Model Level 2 (verbs and status codes used correctly) and skip Level 3 (HATEOAS).
**Visual:**
```
HATEOAS response:
{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Ada",
  "_links": {
    "self":   { "href": "/users/42" },
    "orders": { "href": "/users/42/orders" },
    "update": { "href": "/users/42", "method": "PATCH" },
    "delete": { "href": "/users/42", "method": "DELETE" }
  }
}
client navigates by reading _links, never hardcoding /users/42
```

### Q5. What is the Richardson Maturity Model, and at what level do most APIs sit?
**Answer:** The Richardson Maturity Model (RMM) classifies REST APIs into four levels based on how well they adhere to REST principles. **Level 0** (POX — Plain Old XML/JSON over HTTP): HTTP is just a transport tunnel; one endpoint receives every request via POST, and the operation is encoded in the body. SOAP over HTTP is Level 0. **Level 1** (Resources): the API exposes multiple URLs (one per resource), but everything is still POST — `POST /users/42/delete` instead of `DELETE /users/42`. **Level 2** (HTTP verbs and status codes): the API uses the correct verb for each operation (GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) and returns the correct status code (200/201/204/400/404/422/500). Most production APIs — Stripe, GitHub, Twitter, Slack — sit at Level 2. **Level 3** (HATEOAS): responses include hypermedia links that drive the client; the client never hardcodes URLs. Rarely implemented in practice. The RMM is a useful diagnostic: if your API is at Level 0 or 1, you are leaving REST's benefits (caching, idempotency, uniform interface) on the table. Moving from Level 1 to Level 2 is usually a quick win — change `POST /users/42/delete` to `DELETE /users/42` and start returning proper status codes; you immediately gain HTTP cacheability and idempotency for free.
**Visual:**
```
Level 0: POST /api   body={op: "getUser", id: 42}        (HTTP as tunnel)
Level 1: POST /users/42/delete                          (resources, all POST)
Level 2: DELETE /users/42  -> 204 No Content             (verbs + codes)
Level 3: GET /users/42  ->  { ..., _links: {delete: ...} } (HATEOAS)

Most production APIs (Stripe, GitHub, Twitter): Level 2
```

### Q6. What are safe and idempotent HTTP methods, and why does it matter?
**Answer:** A method is **safe** if it has no side effects (does not change server state) — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Safe methods can be prefetched, cached, and retried without consequence. A method is **idempotent** if calling it N times has the same effect as calling it once — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE. POST and PATCH are neither safe nor idempotent (PATCH can be idempotent if the operation is, like "set name to X", but the spec does not guarantee it). This matters for three reasons. (1) **Caching** — only safe methods can be cached by intermediaries (CDNs, browsers, reverse proxies); POST responses are never cached by default. (2) **Retries** — idempotent methods can be retried automatically by HTTP clients on transient failures (timeout, 5xx) without risk of double-execution; POST requires an `Idempotency-Key` header for safe retry. (3) **Browser behavior** — browsers warn before re-submitting a POST on refresh ("Confirm Form Resubmission") to prevent double-charges; they freely re-issue GET on refresh. Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` exists precisely because POST is not idempotent and payment APIs must survive retries. Understanding this distinction is essential for designing REST APIs that play well with HTTP infrastructure.
**Visual:**
```
                   safe?   idempotent?   cacheable?
   GET             yes     yes           yes
   HEAD            yes     yes           yes
   OPTIONS         yes     yes           no
   POST            no      no            no (unless Cache-Control set)
   PUT             no      yes           no
   PATCH           no      maybe         no
   DELETE          no      yes           no

Implication: GET can be cached and retried freely;
             POST needs Idempotency-Key for safe retry.
```

### Q7. How do conditional GETs with ETag and If-None-Match work, and why use them?
**Answer:** An ETag (entity tag) is a hash of the response body that the server sends with each response — e.g., `ETag: W/"abc123"`. The client stores it and sends it back on the next request as `If-None-Match: W/"abc123"`. The server compares the requested resource's current ETag with the one in the header; if they match, the resource hasn't changed, and the server returns `304 Not Modified` with no body — saving the bandwidth and the CPU time to serialize the response. GitHub's REST API uses this aggressively: every GET response includes an ETag, and clients that poll for changes (CI systems, monitoring tools) send `If-None-Match` on each poll; when nothing has changed, GitHub returns 304 and the poll cycle costs almost nothing. There is also `Last-Modified` / `If-Modified-Since` for time-based conditional requests — coarser but cheaper to compute. ETags can be **strong** (byte-for-byte identical) or **weak** (semantically equivalent, prefixed with `W/`). Weak ETags allow the server to return 304 even if the body differs in insignificant ways (whitespace, key order). Conditional GETs are essential for high-frequency polling clients because they dramatically reduce origin load and bandwidth costs.
**Visual:**
```
Request 1:
   GET /v1/repos/foo/bar
   <- 200 OK, ETag: W/"abc123", body: <10KB JSON>

Request 2 (poll 1 minute later):
   GET /v1/repos/foo/bar
   If-None-Match: W/"abc123"
   <- 304 Not Modified, no body (saves 10KB + serialization CPU)

server's view: compare current ETag to If-None-Match; if equal -> 304.
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are designing the Stripe Charge API. How do you ensure a customer is never double-charged when the network times out between the client and the server?
**Answer:** Use the `Idempotency-Key` header pattern. The client generates a UUID per logical charge (e.g., `key-charge-order-1007`) and sends it with the POST `/v1/charges` request. The server stores the key in a durable store (Postgres or Redis with a 24-hour TTL) along with the response. If the client retries because of a timeout, the server detects the duplicate key, returns the original response (including the original `charge_id`), and does not execute the charge again. The key design decisions: (1) the key store must be durable (Postgres, not in-memory) so it survives server restarts; (2) the key must be checked BEFORE any side effect (database write, downstream API call) to avoid the race where two concurrent retries both pass the check; (3) the key window must exceed the longest plausible retry interval — 24 hours is typical; (4) the client must generate a fresh key per logical operation, not reuse keys across operations. Stripe's actual implementation does exactly this. For idempotent operations (e.g., setting a customer's address to a fixed value), you don't need the key — PUT is already idempotent. The key is for non-idempotent POSTs.
**Visual:**
```
client                     server                    db/redis
   |--- POST /v1/charges   |                          |
   |    Idempotency: k123  |--- check k123 --------->|
   |    body: {amount: 100}|<-- not found ------------|
   |                       |--- create charge ------->|
   |                       |<-- charge_id=ch_xxx -----|
   |                       |--- store k123->ch_xxx -->|
   |<-- 201 + ch_xxx ------|                          |
   (timeout, client never sees 201)
   |--- POST /v1/charges   |                          |
   |    Idempotency: k123  |--- check k123 --------->|
   |                       |<-- found: ch_xxx --------|
   |<-- 201 + ch_xxx (replay, no new charge) --------|
```

### Q2. Your e-commerce API has 1 million products. `GET /products` returns 1000 items per page. Clients complain that page 5000 (`?page=5000`) takes 30 seconds. How do you fix this?
**Answer:** Offset pagination (`LIMIT 1000 OFFSET 5000000`) is O(n) because the database must scan and discard 5M rows before returning the requested 1000. Switch to **cursor-based pagination**: return a cursor (typically the last item's ID or `updated_at`) in the response, and have the client pass it as `?after=<cursor>` on the next request. The server queries `WHERE id > <cursor> ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000`, which uses the primary-key index and is O(log n + 1000). Twitter v2 uses `meta.next_token`; Stripe uses `has_more` + `starting_after`. Trade-offs: (1) cursor pagination cannot jump to an arbitrary page — clients can only paginate forward (and backward if you support a `before` cursor). (2) If items are inserted or deleted between paginations, offset pagination shows duplicates or skips items; cursor pagination is stable. (3) For human-facing UIs that need page numbers, offset may be unavoidable — mitigate with a cap (e.g., max 1000 pages) and a search feature to find specific items. (4) If the sort order is by an indexed non-unique column like `updated_at`, use a compound cursor (`updated_at, id`) to break ties deterministically.
**Visual:**
```
Offset pagination (O(n), slow at high offsets):
   SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000 OFFSET 5000000;
   (DB scans and discards 5M rows)

Cursor pagination (O(log n), fast):
   SELECT * FROM products WHERE id > 5000000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000;
   (uses primary-key index, scans only 1000 rows)

Response: { data: [...], next_cursor: "5001000" }
Next req: GET /products?after=5001000
```

### Q3. Your public REST API receives 10,000 requests per second from a single IP that is scraping your entire catalog. How do you protect the API?
**Answer:** Layered defense. (1) **Rate limiting at the API gateway** — apply a per-IP token bucket (e.g., 100 req/min for anonymous, 1000 req/min for authenticated) at the reverse proxy / API gateway layer (NGINX, Envoy, AWS API Gateway, Kong). Return `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers so well-behaved clients back off. (2) **Per-API-key rate limits** — for authenticated clients, enforce per-key limits (e.g., Stripe's 100 req/sec for live keys, lower for test keys). (3) **WAF / bot detection** — Cloudflare or AWS WAF can fingerprint the scraper's TLS JA3, User-Agent, and behavioral patterns (request timing, headers) and block obvious bots at the edge. (4) **CAPTCHA challenge** — for endpoints that humans use rarely (login, password reset), add a CAPTCHA after N failed attempts. (5) **Cache hot paths** — for read-heavy endpoints that don't need to be fresh (e.g., product catalog), cache at the CDN with `Cache-Control: max-age=60` so the scraper hits the cache and not the origin. (6) **Quota and billing** — for paying customers, enforce daily quotas and charge for overage. (7) **Tarpit / honeypot** — for clearly malicious scrapers, slow responses to a crawl (200 ms → 30 s) to waste their resources. Twitter's API v1.1 famously returned 429 with `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`; GitHub returns 429 with a `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` epoch timestamp.
**Visual:**
```
scraper (1 IP, 10k req/s)
   |
   v
[CDN/WAF] ---- block known-bad JA3/UA, challenge suspicious
   |
   v
[API gateway / reverse proxy]
   |--- per-IP rate limit: 100 req/min  -> 429 (Retry-After: 60)
   |--- per-key rate limit: 1000 req/min -> 429
   |--- daily quota: 100k req/day        -> 403 (quota exhausted)
   |
   v
[REST API]  (only legitimate traffic reaches here)
   |--- cache GET /products (max-age=60) at CDN
```

### Q4. You have a `/v1/orders` resource. Clients want to filter, sort, and expand nested relations (`GET /v1/orders?status=paid&sort=-created_at&expand=user,items`). How do you design this without the API becoming a mess?
**Answer:** Use a consistent query-param convention: `?filter[status]=paid` for filtering, `?sort=-created_at` (minus prefix for descending) for sorting, `?include=user,items` for expanding relations, `?page[size]=50&page[after]=<cursor>` for pagination. This is the JSON:API spec convention — adopted widely because it is consistent and self-documenting. Design decisions: (1) **filtering** — keep simple equality filters as `?status=paid` for ergonomics, but use `filter[...]` for complex operators (`filter[created_at][gte]=2024-01-01`). (2) **sorting** — comma-separated list of fields, minus prefix for descending; never allow sorting by unindexed columns (return 422). (3) **expansion** — `include=user,items` returns the order plus related user and items in a `included` array (JSON:API sideloads to avoid N+1); for GraphQL-like nested expansion, support `include=user.company` (dotted paths). (4) **field selection** — `?fields[orders]=id,total,status` lets clients request only the fields they need, shrinking payload sizes for mobile clients. (5) **validation** — reject unknown query params with 400 (catches typos), enforce max page size (e.g., 100), reject deep expansion (`include=user.posts.comments.author` should be capped at depth 2). Stripe and GitHub both use this style. Trade-off: complex query APIs approach GraphQL in expressiveness — if clients need very flexible queries, just use GraphQL (Phase 2 Topic 11).
**Visual:**
```
GET /v1/orders?filter[status]=paid&sort=-created_at&include=user,items
    &page[size]=50&page[after]=ord_1007&fields[orders]=id,total,status

   filter[status]=paid       -> WHERE status = 'paid'
   sort=-created_at          -> ORDER BY created_at DESC
   include=user,items        -> JOIN user, items (sideload into 'included')
   page[size]=50             -> LIMIT 50
   page[after]=ord_1007      -> WHERE id > 'ord_1007'
   fields[orders]=id,total   -> SELECT id, total, status (no email, no address)
```

### Q5. You are migrating a SOAP/XML internal API to REST/JSON. The SOAP API has 200 operations; the team wants one REST endpoint per operation. How do you push back?
**Answer:** This is the classic Level 0 anti-pattern in REST clothing — using HTTP as a transport tunnel with `POST /api/operation` for everything. Push back by modeling the domain as resources, not operations. SOAP operation `CreateOrder` becomes `POST /v1/orders`; `GetOrder` becomes `GET /v1/orders/{id}`; `CancelOrder` becomes `POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel` (a sub-resource, since cancel is a state transition, not a CRUD on the order itself); `UpdateShippingAddress` becomes `PATCH /v1/orders/{id}` with `{"shipping_address": {...}}`. The benefits: (1) you inherit HTTP's caching (GET can be cached at the CDN), idempotency (PUT/DELETE), and status codes; (2) clients can use generic HTTP tooling (curl, Postman, OpenAPI generators) instead of SOAP-specific stacks; (3) the API surface is smaller and more discoverable. Some SOAP operations do not map cleanly to CRUD — for those, use the "action as sub-resource" pattern (`POST /orders/{id}/cancel`, `POST /orders/{id}/refund`). The team should aim for Richardson Maturity Model Level 2. Trade-off: not every operation fits the resource model perfectly — that's fine, REST is a style, not a religion; the goal is to maximize the use of HTTP's built-in features.
**Visual:**
```
SOAP (Level 0):                     REST (Level 2):
POST /api  body={op: CreateOrder}    POST /v1/orders
POST /api  body={op: GetOrder, id}   GET  /v1/orders/{id}
POST /api  body={op: CancelOrder}    POST /v1/orders/{id}/cancel
POST /api  body={op: UpdateAddr}     PATCH /v1/orders/{id}
                                        body={shipping_address: {...}}

Benefits: HTTP cache, idempotency, status codes, OpenAPI tooling, curl
```

### Q6. Your REST API returns large JSON responses (1 MB each) and mobile clients complain about battery drain and slow loads. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** Multi-layer optimization. (1) **Field selection** — support `?fields=id,name,email` so mobile clients request only the fields they render; cuts payload by 80% in typical cases. (2) **Pagination** — default to 20 items per page for mobile, 100 for desktop; never return unbounded lists. (3) **Compression** — enable gzip or Brotli at the API gateway (NGINX `gzip on;`); Brotli typically achieves 15–25% better compression than gzip on JSON. (4) **Expansion control** — `?expand=user` lets clients opt into nested data only when needed; default to no expansion. (5) **ETag / conditional GET** — mobile clients poll for updates; ETags let them get 304 Not Modified (no body) when nothing changed, saving battery and bandwidth. (6) **HTTP/2** — multiplexes concurrent requests over a single TCP connection, avoiding head-of-line blocking and TCP slow-start on each request; reduces per-request latency by 30–50% on mobile networks. (7) **Diff responses** — for very large rarely-changing resources, support a delta API (send only the fields that changed since the client's last version). (8) **Mobile-specific representation** — consider a separate `/v1/mobile/products` endpoint with a leaner schema, or use Protocol Buffers / gRPC for high-throughput paths. Instagram's mobile API uses a custom binary protocol for exactly this reason. Trade-off: every optimization adds server complexity; measure with real device profiles before optimizing.
**Visual:**
```
Mobile client                    API gateway            REST API
   |--- GET /products            |                      |
   |    ?fields=id,name,thumb    |                      |
   |    &page[size]=20           |                      |
   |    Accept-Encoding: br      |                      |
   |    If-None-Match: W/"a1b2"  |                      |
   |                             |--- forward ------->  |
   |                             |<-- 304 (no body) ----|  (saved 1MB)
   |<-- 304 Not Modified --------|
   |    (saves battery + bandwidth)
```

### Q7. You are designing a public REST API that needs to evolve without breaking thousands of existing clients. What is your deprecation policy?
**Answer:** Five-step policy. (1) **URL versioning from day one** — ship `/v1/`; new breaking changes go to `/v2/`, leaving `/v1/` untouched. (2) **Additive changes only within a version** — add new fields, new endpoints, new optional params freely (these are non-breaking); never remove or rename a field, never change a field's type, never change a status code's meaning. (3) **Sunset headers** — when you plan to deprecate `/v1/`, emit `Sunset: Sat, 31 Dec 2025 23:59:59 GMT` and `Deprecation: true` headers on every `/v1/` response, so client SDKs can warn developers. (4) **Usage telemetry** — log requests by version; only announce a sunset date when usage of the old version drops below a threshold (e.g., 1% of traffic). (5) **Migration runway** — give at least 12 months between announcing sunset and turning off the endpoint; publish a migration guide, run office hours, and proactively reach out to the top users still on v1. Stripe has kept v1 alive since 2014 and has never broken a client; GitHub deprecated v3 in favor of GraphQL but kept v3 running for years; Twitter's abrupt API changes in 2023 are the cautionary tale — breaking changes without runway destroy developer trust. Trade-off: maintaining old versions is engineering cost, but the alternative (breaking clients) is much more expensive in lost customers.
**Visual:**
```
Timeline for /v1/ -> /v2/ migration:
   2024-01-01: v2 released, v1 still supported, additive only
   2024-06-01: v1 usage telemetry drops below 25%
   2024-06-01: v1 starts emitting Sunset + Deprecation headers
   2025-01-01: v1 usage drops below 1%, sunset announced
   2025-12-31: v1 turned off (12 months after announcement)

Each v1 response includes:
   Sunset: Wed, 31 Dec 2025 23:59:59 GMT
   Deprecation: true
   Link: </v2/users>; rel="successor-version"
```

A method is idempotent if calling it N times has the same effect as calling it once — GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE.
POST is not idempotent — POSTing the same payload twice creates two resources.

quiz.explanation: HATEOAS (Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State) is the strictest REST constraint: the server returns hypermedia links in every response, and the client drives state transitions by following those links, never hardcoding URLs. A HATEOAS response looks like {"id": 42, "name": "Ada", "_links": {"self": "/users/42", "orders": "/users/42/orders", "delete": {"href": "/users/42", "method": "DELETE"}}}.

quiz.explanation: The Richardson Maturity Model (RMM) classifies REST APIs into four levels based on how well they adhere to REST principles. Level 0 (POX — Plain Old XML/JSON over HTTP): HTTP is just a transport tunnel; one endpoint receives every request via POST, and the operation is encoded in the body. SOAP over HTTP is Level 0.
